{{Short description|Type of discrete calculus}}
In [[mathematics]], '''calculus on finite weighted graphs''' is a [[discrete calculus]] for functions whose [[Domain of a function|domain]] is the vertex set of a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] with a finite number of [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] and weights associated to the [[Edge (graph theory)|edges]]. This involves formulating discrete [[Operator (mathematics)|operators]] on graphs which are analogous to differential operators in [[calculus]], such as [[Laplacian matrix|graph Laplacians]] (or [[discrete Laplace operator]]s) as discrete versions of the [[Laplacian]], and using these operators to formulate [[differential equation]]s, [[difference equations]], or [[Calculus of variations|variational models]] on graphs which can be interpreted as discrete versions of [[partial differential equations]] or continuum variational models. Such equations and models are important tools to mathematically model, analyze, and process discrete information in many different research fields, e.g., [[image processing]], [[machine learning]], and [[Network theory|network analysis]]. 

In applications, finite weighted graphs represent a finite number of entities by the graph's vertices, any pairwise relationships between these entities by graph edges, and the significance of a relationship by an edge [[weight function]]. Differential equations or difference equations on such graphs can be employed to leverage the graph's structure for tasks such as [[image segmentation]] (where the vertices represent [[pixel]]s and the weighted edges encode pixel similarity based on comparisons of [[Moore neighborhood]]s or larger windows), [[data clustering]], [[Statistical classification|data classification]], or [[Community structure|community]] detection in a [[social network]] (where the vertices represent users of the network, the edges represent links between users, and the weight function indicates the strength of interactions between users).

The main advantage of finite weighted graphs is that by not being restricted to highly regular structures such as discrete [[regular grid]]s, [[lattice graph]]s, or [[Types of mesh|meshes]], they can be applied to represent abstract data with irregular interrelationships.

If a finite weighted graph is geometrically embedded in a [[Euclidean space]], i.e., the graph vertices represent points of this space, then it can be interpreted as a discrete approximation of a related [[nonlocal operator]] in the continuum setting.

== Basic definitions ==
A '''finite weighted graph''' <math>G</math> is defined as a triple <math>G = (V, E, w)</math> for which
* <math>V = \{x_1, \dots, x_n\}, n\in\mathbb{N}</math>, is a finite set of indices denoted as '''graph vertices''' or '''nodes''',
* <math>E \subset V \times V</math> is a finite set of (directed) '''graph edges''' connecting a subset of vertices,
* <math>w \colon E \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> is an '''edge weight function''' defined on the edges of the graph.

In a '''[[directed graph]]''', each edge <math>(x_i,x_j)\in E</math> has a '''start node''' <math>x_i\in V</math> and an '''end node''' <math>x_j\in V</math>. In an '''[[undirected graph]]''' for every edge <math>(x_i,x_j)</math> there exists an edge <math>(x_j,x_i)</math> and the weight function is required to be symmetric, i.e., <math>w(x_i,x_j) = w(x_j,x_i)</math>.{{ref|undirected}} On the remainder of this page, the graphs will be assumed to be undirected, unless specifically stated otherwise. Many of the ideas presented on this page can be generalized to directed graphs.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Luxburg |first1=Ulrike von |last2=Audibert |first2=Jean-Yves |last3=Hein |first3=Matthias |date=2007 |title=Graph Laplacians and their Convergence on Random Neighborhood Graphs |url=http://www.jmlr.org/papers/v8/hein07a.html |journal=Journal of Machine Learning Research |volume=8 |issue=Jun |pages=1325–1368 |issn=1533-7928}}</ref>

The ''edge weight function'' <math>w</math> associates to every edge <math>(x_i,x_j) \in E</math> a real value <math>w(x_i,x_j) > 0</math>. For both mathematical and application specific reasons, the weight function on the edges is often required to be strictly positive and on this page it will be assumed to be so unless specifically stated otherwise. Generalizations of many of the ideas presented on this page to include negatively weighted edges are possible. Sometimes an extension of the domain of the edge weight function to <math>V\times V</math> is considered (with the resulting function still being called the ''edge weight function'') by setting <math>w(x_i,x_j)=0</math> whenever <math>(x_i,x_j) \not\in E</math>.

In applications each ''graph vertex'' <math>x \in V</math> usually represents a single entity in the given data, e.g., elements of a finite data set, pixels in an image, or users in a social network.  A ''graph edge''  represents a relationship between two entities, e.g. pairwise interactions or similarity based on comparisons of geometric neighborhoods (for example of pixels in images) or of another feature, with the edge weight encoding the strength of this relationship. Most commonly used weight functions are normalized to map to values between 0 and 1, i.e., <math> w : E \rightarrow (0,1] </math>.

In the following it is assumed that the considered graphs are [[Connected graph|connected]] without [[Loop (graph theory)|self-loops]] or [[Multigraph|multiple edges]] between vertices. These assumptions are mostly harmless as in many applications each [[Component (graph theory)|connected component]] of a disconnected graph can be treated as a graph in its own right, each appearance of <math>w(x_i,x_i)</math> (which would be nonzero in the presence of self-loops) appears in the presence of another factor which disappears when <math>i=j</math> (see [[#Differential graph operators|the section on differential graph operators]] below), and edge weights can encode similar information as multiple edges could.
 
=== Neighborhood ===
A node <math>x_j \in V</math> is a '''neighbor''' of the node <math>x_i \in V</math> if there exists an edge <math>(x_i,x_j) \in E</math>. 
In terms of notation this relationship can be abbreviated by <math>x_j \sim x_i</math>, which should be read as "<math>x_j</math> is a neighbor of <math>x_i</math>".
Otherwise, if <math>x_j</math> is not a neighbor of <math>x_i</math> one writes <math>x_j\not\sim x_i</math>.
The '''[[neighborhood]]''' <math>\mathcal N(x_i)</math> of a vertex <math>x_i \in V</math> is simply the set of neighbors <math>\mathcal{N}(x_i) := \{ x_j\in V \colon x_j \sim x_i \}</math>.
The '''[[Degree (graph theory)|degree]]''' of a vertex <math>x_i \in V</math> is the weighted size of its neighborhood: 

<math display="block"> \deg(x_i) := \sum_{j\,:\,x_j \sim x_i} w(x_i,x_j).</math>

Note that in the special case where <math> w\equiv 1</math> on <math>E</math> (i.e. the graph is '''[[unweighted graph|unweighted]]''') we have <math> \deg(x_i) := |\mathcal{N}(x_i)|</math>.

=== Space of real vertex functions ===
Let <math>\mathcal{H}(V) := \{f : V \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \}</math> be the '''space of (real) vertex functions'''.  
Since <math>V</math> is a finite set, any vertex function <math>f\in \mathcal{H}(V)</math> can be represented as a <math>n</math>-dimensional vector <math>f \in \mathbb{R}^n</math> (where <math> n:= |V|</math>) and hence the space of vertex functions <math>\mathcal{H}(V)</math> can be identified with an <math>n</math>-dimensional [[Hilbert space]]: <math>\mathcal{H}(V) \cong \mathbb{R}^n</math>. The inner product of <math>\mathcal{H}(V)</math> is defined as:

<math display="block">\langle f, g \rangle_{\mathcal{H}(V)} := \sum_{x_i \in V} f(x_i) g(x_i), \quad \forall f, g \in \mathcal{H}(V).</math>

Furthermore, for any vertex function <math>f \in \mathcal{H}(V)</math> the <math>\ell_p</math>-norm and <math>\ell_\infty</math>-norm of <math>f</math> are defined as:

<math display="block">\|f\|_p = \begin{cases}
  \left( \sum_{x_i\in V} |f(x_i)|^p \right)^\frac{1}{p}, &\text{ for } 1 \leqslant p < \infty \ ,\\
  \max_{x_i\in V}|f(x_i)|,                               &\text{ for } p = \infty \ .
\end{cases}</math>

The <math>\ell_2</math>-norm is induced by the inner product.

In applications vertex functions are useful to label the vertices of the nodes. For example, in graph-based data clustering, each node represents a data point and a [[vertex function]] is used to identify cluster membership of the nodes.

=== Space of real edge functions ===
Analogously to real vertex functions, one can introduce the '''space of real edge functions''' <math>\mathcal{H}(E) := \{F:E \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \}</math>. As any edge function <math>F</math> is defined on a finite set of edges <math>E</math>, it can be represented as a <math>m</math>-dimensional vector <math>F \in \mathbb{R}^{m}</math>, where <math>m := |E|</math>. Hence, the space of edge functions <math>\mathcal{H}(E)</math> can be identified as a <math>m</math>-dimensional Hilbert space, i.e., <math>\mathcal{H}(E) \cong \mathbb{R}^{m}</math>.

One special case of an edge function is the ''normalized edge weight function'' <math>w \colon E \rightarrow (0, 1]</math> introduced above in the [[#Basic definitions|section on basic definitions]]. Similar to that function, any edge function <math>F</math> can be trivially extended to <math>V \times V</math> by setting <math>F(x_i, x_j) := 0 </math> if <math>(x_i, x_j) \not\in E</math>. The space of those extended edge functions is still denoted by <math>\mathcal{H}(E)</math> and can be identified with <math>\mathbb{R}^m</math>, where now <math>m := |V|^2</math>.

The inner product of <math>\mathcal{H}(E)</math> is defined as:

<math display="block"> \langle F, G \rangle_{\mathcal{H}(E)} := \sum_{(x_i, x_j) \in E} F(x_i, x_j) G(x_i, x_j), \quad \forall F, G \in \mathcal{H}(E).</math>

Additionally, for any edge function <math>F \in \mathcal{H}(V)</math> the <math>\ell_p</math>-norm and <math>\ell_\infty</math>-norm of <math>F</math> are defined as:

<math display="block">\|F\|_p = \begin{cases}
  \left(\sum_{(x_i, x_j)\in E} |F(x_i, x_j)|^p\right)^\frac{1}{p} &\text{ for } 1 \leqslant p < \infty \ ,\\
  \max_{(x_i, x_j) \in E}|F(x_i, x_j)|,                           &\text{ for } p = \infty \ .
\end{cases}
</math>

The <math>\ell_2</math>-norm is induced by the inner product.

If one extends the edge set <math>E</math> in a way such that <math>E = V \times V</math> than it becomes clear that <math>\mathcal{H}(E) \cong \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}</math> because <math>\mathcal{H}(V) \cong \mathbb{R}^n</math>. This means that each edge function can be identified with a linear matrix operator.

== Differential graph operators == 
An important ingredient in the calculus on finite weighted graphs is the mimicking of standard differential operators from the continuum setting in the discrete setting of finite weighted graphs.
This allows one to translate well-studied tools from mathematics, such as partial differential equations and variational methods, and make them usable in applications which can best be modeled by a graph.
The fundamental concept which makes this translation possible is the graph gradient, a first-order difference operator on graphs. Based on this one can derive higher-order difference operators, e.g., the graph Laplacian.

=== First-order differential operators ===

==== Weighted differences ====
Let <math>G = (V,E,w)</math> be a finite weighted graph and let <math>f\in \mathcal{H}(V)</math> be a vertex function. 
Then the '''weighted difference''' (or '''weighted graph derivative''') of <math>f</math> along a directed edge <math>(x_i,x_j) \in E</math> is

<math display="block">
  \partial_{x_j}f(x_i) \ := \ \sqrt{w(x_i, x_j)}\left(f(x_j) - f(x_i)\right).
</math>

For any weighted difference the following properties hold:

* <math>\partial_{x_i}f(x_j) = -\partial_{x_j}f(x_i),</math>
* <math>\partial_{x_i}f(x_i) = 0,</math>
* <math>f(x_i) = f(x_j) \Rightarrow \partial_{x_j}f(x_i) = 0.</math>

==== Weighted gradients ====
Based on the notion of weighted differences one defines the '''weighted gradient operator''' on graphs <math>\nabla_w: \mathcal{H}(V) \rightarrow \mathcal{H}(E)</math> as

<math display="block">
  (\nabla_w f)(x_i, x_j) \ = \ \partial_{x_j}f(x_i).
</math>

This is a [[linear operator]].

To measure the ''local variation'' of a vertex function <math>f</math> in a vertex <math>x_i \in V</math> one can restrict the gradient <math>\nabla_w f</math> of <math>f</math> to all directed edges starting in <math>x_i</math> and using the <math>\ell_p</math>-norm of this edge function, i.e.,

<math display="block">\|(\nabla_w f)(x_i,\cdot)\|_{\ell_p} = \begin{cases}
  \left(\sum_{x_j \sim x_i}w(x_i, x_j)^\frac{p}{2}|f(x_j) - f(x_i)|^p\right)^\frac{1}{p} &\text{ for } 1 \leq p < \infty,\\
  \max_{x_j \sim x_i} \sqrt{w(x_i, x_j)}|f(x_j) - f(x_i)|                                &\text{ for } p = \infty.
\end{cases}</math>

==== Weighted divergence ====
The '''[[Transpose of a linear map|adjoint operator]]''' <math>\nabla_w^*\colon\mathcal{H}(E)\rightarrow \mathcal{H}(V)</math> of the weighted gradient operator is a linear operator defined by 

<math display="block">
\langle \nabla_wf,G\rangle_{\mathcal{H}(E)} = \langle f,\nabla_w^*G\rangle_{\mathcal{H}(V)} \quad \text{ for all } f\in \mathcal{H}(V), G\in \mathcal{H}(E).
</math>

For undirected graphs with a symmetric weight function <math>w \in \mathcal{H}(E)</math> the adjoint operator <math>\nabla_w^*</math> of a function <math>F\in \mathcal{H}(E)</math> at a vertex <math>x_i\in V</math> has the following form:

<math display="block">
  \left(\nabla_w^*F\right)(x_i) \ = \ \frac{1}{2}\sum_{x_j\sim x_i}{\sqrt{w(x_i, x_j)}(F(x_j, x_i) - F(x_i, x_j))}.
</math>

One can then define the '''weighted divergence operator''' on graphs via the adjoint operator as <math>\operatorname{div}_w := -\nabla_w^*</math>. The divergence on a graph measures the net outflow of an edge function in each vertex of the graph.

=== Second-order differential operators ===
==== Graph Laplace operator ====
The '''weighted graph Laplacian''' <math>\Delta_w : \mathcal{H}(V) \rightarrow \mathcal{H}(V)</math> is a well-studied operator in the graph setting. Mimicking the relationship <math>\operatorname{div}(\nabla f) = \Delta f</math> of the Laplace operator in the continuum setting, the weighted graph Laplacian can be derived for any vertex <math>x_i \in V</math> as:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
  (\operatorname{div}_w(\nabla_w f))(x_i)
    &= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{x_j \sim x_i}\sqrt{w(x_i, x_j)}(\nabla_w f(x_j, x_i) - \nabla_w f(x_i, x_j))\\
    &= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{x_j \sim x_i}\sqrt{w(x_i, x_j)}\left(\sqrt{w(x_i, x_j)}(f(x_j) - f(x_i)) - \sqrt{w(x_j, x_i)}(f(x_i) - f(x_j))\right)\\
    &= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{x_j \sim x_i}w(x_i, x_j)(2f(x_j) - 2f(x_i))\\
    &= \sum_{x_j \sim x_i}w(x_i, x_j)(f(x_j) - f(x_i)) \ =: \ (\Delta_w f)(x_i).
\end{align}</math>

Note that one has to assume that the graph <math>G</math> is undirected and has a symmetric weight function <math>w(x_i, x_j) = w(x_j, x_i)</math> for this representation.

==== Graph p-Laplace operators ====
The continuous <math>p</math>-Laplace operator is a second-order differential operator that can be well-translated to finite weighted graphs. 
It allows the translation of various partial differential equations, e.g., the heat equation, to the graph setting.

Based on the first-order partial difference operators on graphs one can formally derive a family of '''weighted graph <math>p</math>-Laplace operators''' <math>\Delta_{w,p} \colon \mathcal{H}(V) \rightarrow \mathcal{H}(V)</math> for <math>1 \leq p < \infty </math> by minimization of the discrete <math>p</math>-Dirichlet energy functional

<math display="block">
  E(f) \ := \ \frac{1}{p} \sum_{x_i \in V} \|\nabla_w f(x_i,\cdot)\|_{\ell_p}^p.
</math>

The necessary optimality conditions for a minimizer of the energy functional <math>E</math> lead to the following definition of the graph <math>p</math>-Laplacian:

<math display="block">
  (\Delta_{w,p} f)(x_i) \ := \ \sum_{x_j\sim x_i} w(x_i, x_j)^\frac{p}{2} |f(x_j) - f(x_i)|^{p-2} (f(x_j) - f(x_i)).
</math>

Note that the graph Laplace operator is a special case of the graph <math>p</math>-Laplace operator for <math>p = 2</math>, i.e., 

<math display="block">
  (\Delta_{w,2} f)(x_i) \ = \ (\Delta_w f)(x_i) \ = \ \sum_{x_j\sim x_i} w(x_i, x_j) (f(x_j) - f(x_i)).
</math>

== Applications ==
Calculus on finite weighted graphs is used in a wide range of applications from different fields such as image processing, machine learning, and network analysis.
A non-exhaustive list of tasks in which finite weighted graphs have been employed is:
* [[image denoising]]<ref name="Gilboa">{{Cite journal |last1=Gilboa |first1=Guy |last2=Osher |first2=Stanley |s2cid=7153727 |date=2009 |title=Nonlocal Operators with Applications to Image Processing |journal=Multiscale Modeling & Simulation |language=en |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=1005–1028 |doi=10.1137/070698592 |issn=1540-3459}}</ref><ref name="Elmoataz_denoising">{{Cite journal |last1=Elmoataz |first1=A. |last2=Lezoray |first2=O. |last3=Bougleux |first3=S. |date=2008 |title=Nonlocal Discrete Regularization on Weighted Graphs: A Framework for Image and Manifold Processing |journal=IEEE Transactions on Image Processing |volume=17 |issue=7 |pages=1047–1060 |doi=10.1109/TIP.2008.924284 |pmid=18586614 |bibcode=2008ITIP...17.1047E |s2cid=9687337 |issn=1057-7149|citeseerx=10.1.1.491.1516 }}</ref>
* [[image segmentation]]<ref name="Elmoataz_Eikonal">{{Cite journal |last1=Desquesnes |first1=Xavier |last2=Elmoataz |first2=Abderrahim |last3=Lézoray |first3=Olivier |date=2013 |title=Eikonal Equation Adaptation on Weighted Graphs: Fast Geometric Diffusion Process for Local and Non-local Image and Data Processing |journal=Journal of Mathematical Imaging and Vision |language=en |volume=46 |issue=2 |pages=238–257 |doi=10.1007/s10851-012-0380-9 |bibcode=2013JMIV...46..238D |s2cid=254643702 |issn=0924-9907|url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00932510/file/Desquesnes-jmiv2012.pdf }}</ref>

== Notes ==
:1.{{note|undirected}}Note that a slightly different definition of ''undirected  graph'' is also in use, which considers an undirected edge to be a [[two-set]] (set with two distinct elements) <math>\{x_i,x_j\}</math> instead of a pair of [[ordered pair]]s <math>(x_i,x_j)</math> and <math>(x_j,x_i)</math>. Here the latter description is needed, as it is required to allow edge functions in <math>\mathcal{H}(E)</math> (see [[#Space of edge functions|the section about the space of edge functions]]) to take different values on <math>(x_i,x_j)</math> and <math>(x_j,x_i)</math>.
